Security misconfiguration
Last reviewed 2026-10-04 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can audit a deployed API for the settings OWASP API8:2023 lists, say what an error response, a method list, a TLS configuration and a set of response headers should look like and which source says so, explain what a redirect and HSTS do not do for an API client, and show that an environment still matches its baseline.

Before you start. You should be able to read an HTTP request and response and a Python dict. You should know that TLS encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity to the client. The primer, Security concepts for the course, covers that.
Published lesson 30 of 31Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleHotels installs a booking API from a framework's quick-start guide and puts it on the internet at api.examplehotels.example. The company is fictional. The application code is correct: it checks a token before it returns a booking. Nobody changed a setting, so every setting is whatever the framework shipped with.

An attacker with an ordinary guest account sends a request with a booking id of abc. The reply is a debug page. It holds a stack trace (the list of function calls that were running when the code failed), the file path of the application, the SQL query that was being built, and the server's name and version. The attacker looks up that version, finds a published flaw, and now has a target. Then they try the rest of the defaults: a DELETE that nobody meant to offer, a /debug/config page, the vendor's documented default account, and the same API on plain HTTP.

None of this is a bug in the code. OWASP calls it security misconfiguration, API8:2023, and says it "can happen at any level of the API stack, from the network level to the application level." The table shows four configurations of the same code. Every cell is a result the lab in section 7 measures.

The last row needs an attacker who can see the network between the client and the server. The third column is the one people get wrong, and section 5 covers it.
2. Why it works

Software ships with defaults chosen so that it works the first time someone runs it. That is a reasonable goal for a developer's laptop and the wrong one for a public listener (a port that accepts connections from the internet). Four broken assumptions keep the defaults in place:

  • "The code passed review, so the service is safe." A review of the code reads none of the settings below. API8:2023 lists eight ways an API might be vulnerable, and a deployment can get every one of them wrong with no change to the application code: missing hardening or wrong cloud permissions, missing patches, unnecessary features such as HTTP verbs, servers in a chain that process a request differently, missing TLS, missing security or cache directives, a missing or wrong CORS policy, and error messages that include stack traces.
  • "An error message helps the caller." It helps the attacker more. The OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet says an attack begins with a reconnaissance phase in which the attacker gathers technical information, "often name and version properties", and that unhandled errors assist it. OWASP Top 10:2025 A10 describes the next step: the attacker "continues to force errors in order to use the sensitive system information to create a better SQL injection attack."
  • "If something goes wrong, the request will fail." Only if someone decided that. An exception that is caught and ignored lets the request carry on without the check that raised it. That is failing open. A10 lists it by name, as CWE-636, Not Failing Securely.
  • "Production matches what we tested." A setting changed by hand during an incident stays changed. This is configuration drift, and nothing reports it unless something compares the environment with its baseline.

Old versions of the API and old TLS versions fail the same way: they stay enabled because turning them off might break a caller nobody can name. RFC 8996 gives that as one of its reasons for deprecating TLS 1.0 and 1.1: "Support for four TLS protocol versions increases the likelihood of misconfiguration."
3. The control
The control is a written baseline, applied the same way everywhere, and an audit that probes the running service. In order:

1. Return a generic error and keep the detail on the server. One global exception handler catches whatever the code did not. The client gets a status code, a fixed title and an identifier for this occurrence, called a correlation ID. The exception goes to the server log under the same identifier. RFC 9457 defines a JSON format for this, problem details, with the media type application/problem+json. Section 4 has the limits of that RFC.
  2. Fail closed. When a check cannot complete, the answer is no. An error in authentication or authorization code must never turn into "allowed". This is deny by default applied to the error path.
  3. Allow only the methods each route needs. Keep an allowlist of methods per route. RFC 9110 section 9.1 says a server should answer 405 (Method Not Allowed) for a method it knows but does not allow on that resource, and 501 (Not Implemented) for one it does not recognize. Section 15.5.6 requires a 405 response to carry an Allow header listing the supported methods. Turn TRACE off: it asks the server to send the request back, headers included.
  4. Remove what the API does not use. Debug endpoints, sample pages and default accounts come out of the build. Management endpoints move to a listener the internet cannot reach, with their own strong authentication.
  5. Use TLS on every hop and refuse plain HTTP. API8 asks for an encrypted channel between the client, the API server and "any downstream/upstream components", "regardless of whether it is an internal or public-facing API." Disable SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. Offer TLS 1.3. If you keep TLS 1.2, restrict its cipher suites (the named combinations of key exchange, encryption and hash that a connection may use). Section 4 gives the sources.
  6. Send the response headers an API needs. Cache-Control: no-store on any response with personal or secret data, a correct Content-Type on every response that has content, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, which tells a browser to follow the declared type and not guess one from the content. Send no version in the Server header. Send HSTS if a browser may ever call the API.
  7. Make every server in the chain read a request the same way. A proxy that blocks /admin and a backend that treats //admin as /admin do not enforce the same rule. API8 asks that all servers in the chain "process incoming requests in a uniform manner to avoid desync issues" and gives no example. The double slash, here and in Part E of the lab, is this project's illustration, not OWASP's.
  8. Patch, and know what you run. Compare each component's version with the vendor's first fixed version, on a schedule.
  9. Build every environment from the baseline and audit it automatically. Compare each environment with the baseline, not only with another environment, and probe the running service as well as reading its settings.
Where each setting lives

Some of this ground is taught elsewhere and only linked here. From API8's lists: CORS policy is Module 17, CORS. API8 also says to restrict incoming content types and to define and enforce response schemas, error responses included. This module does not teach either. The nearest lesson is Module 13, Request and response contracts, which covers checking request bodies and giving every rejection one error shape. Two neighbours are not on API8's lists: old versions that are still reachable are API9:2023 and Module 18, Versioning and deprecation, and paths that reach a service without passing the gateway are Module 12, Gateway enforcement.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultWhat the sources say, and when to change it
Error bodyRFC 9457 problem details with type about:blank, the status, the standard title and an instance that carries the correlation IDRFC 9457 defines a format. It does not require an API to use it: section 1 says problem details "are (naturally) not the only way to convey the details of a problem in HTTP". What it does say about content is in section 4, "Problem details are not a debugging tool for the underlying implementation", and section 5 encourages generators that provide links to occurrence information to avoid making a stack dump available through the HTTP interface. Define your own problem types for errors a client can act on. The correlation ID is this project's use of instance, which the RFC defines as a URI reference that identifies the specific occurrence.
Minimum TLS versionTLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 enabled, nothing olderRFC 9325 section 3.1.1 says implementations must not negotiate SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. RFC 8996 sections 4 and 5 say the same of TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Drop TLS 1.2 once every caller supports 1.3: RFC 9325 section 1 says a provider "might decide to disable TLS 1.2 entirely and offer only TLS 1.3."
TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 supportOffer TLS 1.3 and prefer itRFC 9325 section 3.1.1, as published in 2022, says implementations must support TLS 1.2 and should support TLS 1.3, and must prefer 1.3 when they have it. RFC 9852 (July 2026) changes two of those for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported, and TLS 1.2 may be. Its rule is addressed to protocol specifications: "Any new protocol that uses TLS MUST specify TLS 1.3 as its default." It does not tell an existing HTTP API to turn TLS 1.2 off. TLS 1.3 itself is RFC 9846.
TLS 1.2 cipher suitesThe four suites RFC 9325 section 4.2 recommends, all ECDHE with AES-GCMRFC 10015 (July 2026) raises three of RFC 9325's "should not" rules to "must not" for TLS 1.2: static RSA key exchange, ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman and non-ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman. Non-ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman stays at "should not". RFC 9325 section 4.1 already forbids NULL and RC4 suites. Change the list only to remove suites.
Plain HTTPListener offThe OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet: "API-only endpoints should disable HTTP altogether and only support encrypted connections. When that is not possible, API endpoints should fail requests made over unencrypted HTTP connections instead of redirecting them." RFC 6797 section 7.2 says an HSTS host should answer plain HTTP with a permanent redirect. That advice is written for sites that people visit in a browser. Redirect only for those.
HSTSStrict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 on HTTPS responsesRFC 6797 section 6.1.1 requires the max-age directive and section 7.2 forbids sending the header over plain HTTP. RFC 9325 section 3.2 says web servers should use HSTS. The value is one year. RFC 6797 uses it in an example (section 6.2) and neither RFC recommends a figure, so the choice is this project's. It only affects clients that implement HSTS, which in practice means browsers. Start with a short max-age when a mistake would lock users out.
MethodsAn allowlist per route, TRACE offAPI8: "Be specific about which HTTP verbs each API can be accessed by: all other HTTP verbs should be disabled (e.g. HEAD)." RFC 9110 section 9.1 says "All general-purpose servers MUST support the methods GET and HEAD", so the lab keeps HEAD next to GET. If a browser calls the API across origins, the route also needs OPTIONS for the preflight.
CachingCache-Control: no-store on every responseRFC 9111 section 5.2.2.5: with no-store, "a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response". Relax it only for responses that hold nothing private and that you want cached.
Server bannerNo Server header, or a value with no versionRFC 9110 section 10.2.4 says an origin server should not send "needlessly fine-grained detail". The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet: "Remove this header or set non-informative values." Section 5 says how little this buys.
EnvironmentsIdentical settings, different credentials and hostnamesOWASP Top 10:2025 A02: "Development, QA, and production environments should all be configured identically, with different credentials used in each environment." List the settings that are meant to differ, and keep that list short.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that on the day of the audit, the running service refused each probe, and that its settings matched the baseline. That is all a clean audit says.

Doesn't prove the code is right. The lab's hardened API still fails on a booking id of abc. The configuration hides the detail and denies the request. It does not fix the missing input check. A10 says to catch errors where they occur and to keep a global handler "in case there is ever something we have missed". The handler is the backstop, not the fix.

Doesn't make a hidden version safe. RFC 9110 section 17.12 says that product information can in theory help an attacker, and then: "in practice, attackers tend to try all potential holes regardless of the apparent software versions being used". Removing the banner is cheap and worth doing. Patching is the control.

no-store is an instruction, not a guarantee. RFC 9111 says of it: "This directive is not a reliable or sufficient mechanism for ensuring privacy." A cache that is broken or hostile can ignore it.

A redirect and HSTS do not protect an API client. A redirect from http to https is an answer, and the server can only answer a request it has already received. The token in that request crossed the network in clear text first. HSTS exists to stop a browser sending that first request the next time, and it only works in a client that implements it. RFC 6797 section 14.2: "Non-conformant user agents ignore the Strict-Transport-Security header field". A script, a mobile app's HTTP library or another server will follow whatever URL it was configured with. Even a conformant client is exposed on its first visit, which RFC 6797 section 14.6 calls the bootstrap MITM vulnerability (MITM is short for man in the middle, an attacker placed between the client and the server). For an API, the control is that nothing answers on plain HTTP and every documented URL starts with https. A closed listener stops an attacker who can only watch the network. One who can answer in the server's place can still collect what a client sends to an http URL, which is why the client's URL is half of the control. Part D of the lab counts the tokens that leak each way.

Most browser security headers do nothing for a non-browser client. The OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet says that if an API is only consumed by non-browser clients, "most of these headers will have no effect since they are directives for browsers." Send the short list in section 3 anyway. It costs nothing, and you rarely know every client. Cookie attributes and request forgery belong to Module 28, Browser sessions, cookies and CSRF.

A comparison of two environments is not an audit. Two environments with the same wrong setting are identical. Part C of the lab shows two default installs that differ in nothing and have 15 findings each.
6. Prove it

A hardened deployment must pass every one of these, in every environment. If one fails, the control is broken:

  • A request that makes the code raise an error returns a generic body with no stack trace, file path, query text or version, and the server log holds the detail under the identifier in the body.
  • A malformed, truncated or oversized credential is refused. It never falls through to the handler.
  • Every method that is not on a route's allowlist returns 405 with an Allow header, TRACE included, and has no effect. An unknown method returns 501.
  • /debug, sample pages and framework consoles return 404 on the public listener.
  • The vendor's default account is refused on every listener, and the management login is not reachable from the public listener at all.
  • A response with personal data carries Cache-Control: no-store, a correct Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
  • A connection to the plain HTTP port is refused. If a redirect is unavoidable, no HSTS header appears on the plain HTTP response.
  • A client that offers only TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 fails the handshake. No TLS 1.2 suite with static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange is selected.
  • A path written as //admin/login gets the same answer from the edge as /admin/login.
  • No component is behind its first fixed version.
  • The settings of each environment differ from the baseline only in the keys listed as per-environment, and the list is reviewed when it changes.

Download labs/misconfiguration_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3.

The API is a Python class driven by a configuration dict, and the auditor is a second class that calls it. The same application code runs in every part. Nothing opens a socket. TLS is a tuple of version names and a tuple of cipher suite names compared with the RFCs' rules, and no handshake takes place. The leaked error page is built from fixed strings, so it is not a real traceback, and the correlation ID is a counter where a real service would use a random value. The cipher suite check matches name prefixes, which is enough for the suites in the lab; RFC 10015 section 5 lists the affected suites one by one. The HSTS agent in Part D models two rules of RFC 6797: it notes a host from a header received over HTTPS (section 8.1) and rewrites http to https for a noted host (section 8.3). It does not follow redirects, and it leaves out includeSubDomains, max-age=0, preloaded lists and certificate errors. The vendor's default account is a placeholder pair, not any real product's default. Responses carry only the headers this module is about: RFC 9110 section 15.5.2 requires a 401 to carry WWW-Authenticate, and the lab's 401 does not.

Four results are worth a second look. Checks 22 to 24 are the fail open case: with no Authorization header the default install answers 401, as it should, but a header that the parser cannot split answers 200, and the server's own log says the error was ignored. Checks 56 and 57 are the same request against the hardened configuration: 500, and no booking in the body.

Checks 29 and 30 show both halves of an error. The client gets four fields, and none of them describes the code. The exception type and the path are in the server log under the same identifier. Module 30, Logging, detection and response, covers what to do with that log.

Checks 63 and 64 are the reason to compare with a baseline. Two default installs differ from each other in nothing. Each differs from the hardened baseline in 17 settings.

Checks 65 to 76 count tokens. With a redirect in place, a plain API client leaks its token on every call (checks 68 and 74). A client that implements HSTS leaks it on its first visit (check 70), stops once it has seen the header over HTTPS (check 72), and starts again when max-age runs out (check 73). The count in check 74 is 4 because it includes that request and the plain client's second call. With the listener off, the count stays at zero (check 76).

  • In HARDENED, change "cache_control": "no-store" to "no-cache". The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet warns about this one: no-cache "does not prevent caching; it allows caches to store responses."
8. Check your understanding

An API answers every plain HTTP request with a 301 to the https URL. A partner's script is configured with the http URL. What has the redirect protected?

Nothing in that request. The script sent its token in clear text, and the server could only redirect after it arrived. If the script follows the redirect, the call succeeds and nobody notices. Refusing the connection makes the mistake fail on the first test.

Your error responses now follow RFC 9457. Is the information leak fixed?

Not by the format. RFC 9457 defines where fields go. It does not stop a generator putting a stack trace in detail. The RFC says detail "ought to focus on helping the client correct the problem, rather than giving debugging information", and its security considerations say the details given must be scrutinized. The fix is what you put in the body, and one global handler so that no error path is missed.

Staging and production have identical configuration files. Is production hardened?

You do not know yet. They may be identical and wrong. Compare each with the written baseline, then probe the running service, because a setting can also be overridden at run time without the file changing.

RFC 9852 says new protocols must require TLS 1.3. Must you disable TLS 1.2 on an existing API today?

The RFC does not say so. It changes RFC 9325's rules for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported and TLS 1.2 may be. What every deployment must not do is negotiate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or SSL, and, since RFC 10015, select static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange in TLS 1.2. Dropping TLS 1.2 is a choice you make when your callers allow it.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The handler caught the error and carried on, so the check that raised it never ran. An error in a security check has to end in a refusal.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. The token check exists and works for a well-formed header. The fault is what the configuration does when that check raises an error: it allows the request instead of refusing it.

Quick check

An error in the wrong direction

An API returns 401 when the Authorization header is missing and 200 when the header is present but cannot be parsed. Which rule is broken?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/misconfiguration_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The published run prints 93 lines and ends all 80 lab checks passed. None of the edits needs a package.

1. The plain HTTP listener redirects

A partner complains that http URLs stopped working. In HARDENED, change "http_listener": "off" to "redirect".

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The lab exits 1. A redirect is an answer to a request that has already been sent, and the lab counts the credentials in those requests.
  • Check 49 does print 301, but check 58 still prints []. The auditor's plain-http probe only reports a listener that serves content with a 200. An audit finds what its probes look for, which is a reason to read them.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Checks 49 and 75 go from connection refused to 301, and checks 50 and 76 go from 0 to 1. The guest token crossed the network in clear text before the server could answer, and the full audit in check 58 did not notice. Check cfg-03 in the Reference layer asks for a refused connection for this reason.
  • That is the "serve" setting, which the default install uses. With "redirect" the booking is not in the reply. The token still was in the request.

2. Authentication errors are allowed through again

The token service has an outage, and someone decides the API should stay up when authentication code fails. In HARDENED, change "on_auth_error": "deny" to "allow".

How many checks fail, and what does check 56 print?

Every option, and why
  • Check 56 does print 200, but it is not alone. The setting is part of the baseline, so every environment built from it inherits the change, and the audits and the settings count see it too.
  • Correct. Exit 1, six failures. Check 56 goes from 500 to 200 and check 57 from False to True: the booking is in the body. Check 58 goes from [] to ['fail-open'], check 61 the same, check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'fail-open'], and check 64 from 17 to 16, because the baseline now agrees with the default install on one more setting. Check cfg-02 in the Reference layer is the rule this breaks.
  • A 401 would be a refusal. The "allow" branch returns a caller named unverified, which is not None, so the handler carries on and serves the booking.
  • The auditor sends one. Check 56 uses an Authorization header with a scheme and no token, which is all it takes.

3. The drifted setting is declared a per-environment difference

The comparison in Part C keeps reporting debug_errors. To quiet it, someone adds the key to the list of settings that are meant to differ:

PER_ENVIRONMENT_KEYS = ("hostname", "debug_errors")
What does Part C print now?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 60 goes from ['debug_errors'] to []. The comparison is now silent, and production still returns a stack trace, which the probe behind check 62 still finds. An exception list is itself configuration. Check cfg-10 in the Reference layer asks for it to be short and reviewed, and for the running service to be probed as well.
  • Check 62 does not read the list. It sends a request with a bad booking id to production and looks at the body that comes back.
  • Check 59 is the comparison with nothing left out, so it still prints ['debug_errors', 'hostname'].
  • The lab compares check 60 with the value it expects, so quieting the comparison fails the run.

4. TLS 1.1 is turned back on for one old client

In HARDENED, change "tls_versions": ("TLS1.2", "TLS1.3") to ("TLS1.1", "TLS1.2", "TLS1.3").

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 51 changes, and so does every audit of an environment built from this baseline.
  • Check 52 still prints protocol_version alert. The client in that check offers only TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.0 is still off.
  • Check 53 still prints TLS1.3. The lab's negotiate picks the highest version both sides have, and a client that offers TLS 1.2 and 1.3 is not affected by a lower version being enabled. The exposure is to clients that offer nothing better.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 51 goes from [] to ['TLS1.1'], checks 58 and 61 from [] to ['tls-versions'], and check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'tls-versions']. No request in the lab behaves differently, which is why this kind of change survives: nothing breaks, and one exception for one client becomes the setting for every environment. Check cfg-04 in the Reference layer is the rule.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can audit a deployed API for the settings OWASP API8:2023 lists, say what an error response, a method list, a TLS configuration and a set of response headers should look like and which source says so, explain what a redirect and HSTS do not do for an API client, and show that an environment still matches its baseline.

Before you start. You should be able to read an HTTP request and response and a Python dict. You should know that TLS encrypts a connection and proves the server's identity to the client. The primer, Security concepts for the course, covers that.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExampleHotels installs a booking API from a framework's quick-start guide and puts it on the internet at api.examplehotels.example. The company is fictional. The application code is correct: it checks a token before it returns a booking. Nobody changed a setting, so every setting is whatever the framework shipped with.

An attacker with an ordinary guest account sends a request with a booking id of abc. The reply is a debug page. It holds a stack trace (the list of function calls that were running when the code failed), the file path of the application, the SQL query that was being built, and the server's name and version. The attacker looks up that version, finds a published flaw, and now has a target. Then they try the rest of the defaults: a DELETE that nobody meant to offer, a /debug/config page, the vendor's documented default account, and the same API on plain HTTP.

None of this is a bug in the code. OWASP calls it security misconfiguration, API8:2023, and says it "can happen at any level of the API stack, from the network level to the application level." The table shows four configurations of the same code. Every cell is a result the lab in section 7 measures.

The attacker tries toDefault installHardenedHardened, but plain HTTP redirectsHardened, but debug errors left on
Read a stack trace, a query and a version from an errorWorksBlockedBlockedWorks

Read a booking with a malformed credentialWorksBlockedBlockedBlocked
Make a client that offers only TLS 1.0 connectWorksBlockedBlockedBlocked

The last row needs an attacker who can see the network between the client and the server. The third column is the one people get wrong, and section 5 covers it.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Software ships with defaults chosen so that it works the first time someone runs it. That is a reasonable goal for a developer's laptop and the wrong one for a public listener (a port that accepts connections from the internet). Four broken assumptions keep the defaults in place:

  • "The code passed review, so the service is safe." A review of the code reads none of the settings below. API8:2023 lists eight ways an API might be vulnerable, and a deployment can get every one of them wrong with no change to the application code: missing hardening or wrong cloud permissions, missing patches, unnecessary features such as HTTP verbs, servers in a chain that process a request differently, missing TLS, missing security or cache directives, a missing or wrong CORS policy, and error messages that include stack traces.
  • "An error message helps the caller." It helps the attacker more. The OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet says an attack begins with a reconnaissance phase in which the attacker gathers technical information, "often name and version properties", and that unhandled errors assist it. OWASP Top 10:2025 A10 describes the next step: the attacker "continues to force errors in order to use the sensitive system information to create a better SQL injection attack."
  • "If something goes wrong, the request will fail." Only if someone decided that. An exception that is caught and ignored lets the request carry on without the check that raised it. That is failing open. A10 lists it by name, as CWE-636, Not Failing Securely.
  • "Production matches what we tested." A setting changed by hand during an incident stays changed. This is configuration drift, and nothing reports it unless something compares the environment with its baseline.

Old versions of the API and old TLS versions fail the same way: they stay enabled because turning them off might break a caller nobody can name. RFC 8996 gives that as one of its reasons for deprecating TLS 1.0 and 1.1: "Support for four TLS protocol versions increases the likelihood of misconfiguration."

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
The control is a written baseline, applied the same way everywhere, and an audit that probes the running service. In order:

  1. Return a generic error and keep the detail on the server. One global exception handler catches whatever the code did not. The client gets a status code, a fixed title and an identifier for this occurrence, called a correlation ID. The exception goes to the server log under the same identifier. RFC 9457 defines a JSON format for this, problem details, with the media type application/problem+json. Section 4 has the limits of that RFC.
  2. Fail closed. When a check cannot complete, the answer is no. An error in authentication or authorization code must never turn into "allowed". This is deny by default applied to the error path.
  3. Allow only the methods each route needs. Keep an allowlist of methods per route. RFC 9110 section 9.1 says a server should answer 405 (Method Not Allowed) for a method it knows but does not allow on that resource, and 501 (Not Implemented) for one it does not recognize. Section 15.5.6 requires a 405 response to carry an Allow header listing the supported methods. Turn TRACE off: it asks the server to send the request back, headers included.
  4. Remove what the API does not use. Debug endpoints, sample pages and default accounts come out of the build. Management endpoints move to a listener the internet cannot reach, with their own strong authentication.
  5. Use TLS on every hop and refuse plain HTTP. API8 asks for an encrypted channel between the client, the API server and "any downstream/upstream components", "regardless of whether it is an internal or public-facing API." Disable SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. Offer TLS 1.3. If you keep TLS 1.2, restrict its cipher suites (the named combinations of key exchange, encryption and hash that a connection may use). Section 4 gives the sources.
  6. Send the response headers an API needs. Cache-Control: no-store on any response with personal or secret data, a correct Content-Type on every response that has content, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, which tells a browser to follow the declared type and not guess one from the content. Send no version in the Server header. Send HSTS if a browser may ever call the API.
  7. Make every server in the chain read a request the same way. A proxy that blocks /admin and a backend that treats //admin as /admin do not enforce the same rule. API8 asks that all servers in the chain "process incoming requests in a uniform manner to avoid desync issues" and gives no example. The double slash, here and in Part E of the lab, is this project's illustration, not OWASP's.
  8. Patch, and know what you run. Compare each component's version with the vendor's first fixed version, on a schedule.
  9. Build every environment from the baseline and audit it automatically. Compare each environment with the baseline, not only with another environment, and probe the running service as well as reading its settings.

Where each setting lives

ClientRequest pathNot on the request pathMust refuse

Some of this ground is taught elsewhere and only linked here. From API8's lists: CORS policy is Module 17, CORS. API8 also says to restrict incoming content types and to define and enforce response schemas, error responses included. This module does not teach either. The nearest lesson is Module 13, Request and response contracts, which covers checking request bodies and giving every rejection one error shape. Two neighbours are not on API8's lists: old versions that are still reachable are API9:2023 and Module 18, Versioning and deprecation, and paths that reach a service without passing the gateway are Module 12, Gateway enforcement.

sections.heading: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.heading_text: 4. Defaults and when to change them
sections.html:
DecisionStarting defaultWhat the sources say, and when to change it
Error bodyRFC 9457 problem details with type about:blank, the status, the standard title and an instance that carries the correlation IDRFC 9457 defines a format. It does not require an API to use it: section 1 says problem details "are (naturally) not the only way to convey the details of a problem in HTTP". What it does say about content is in section 4, "Problem details are not a debugging tool for the underlying implementation", and section 5 encourages generators that provide links to occurrence information to avoid making a stack dump available through the HTTP interface. Define your own problem types for errors a client can act on. The correlation ID is this project's use of instance, which the RFC defines as a URI reference that identifies the specific occurrence.
Minimum TLS versionTLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 enabled, nothing olderRFC 9325 section 3.1.1 says implementations must not negotiate SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. RFC 8996 sections 4 and 5 say the same of TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Drop TLS 1.2 once every caller supports 1.3: RFC 9325 section 1 says a provider "might decide to disable TLS 1.2 entirely and offer only TLS 1.3."
TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 supportOffer TLS 1.3 and prefer itRFC 9325 section 3.1.1, as published in 2022, says implementations must support TLS 1.2 and should support TLS 1.3, and must prefer 1.3 when they have it. RFC 9852 (July 2026) changes two of those for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported, and TLS 1.2 may be. Its rule is addressed to protocol specifications: "Any new protocol that uses TLS MUST specify TLS 1.3 as its default." It does not tell an existing HTTP API to turn TLS 1.2 off. TLS 1.3 itself is RFC 9846.
TLS 1.2 cipher suitesThe four suites RFC 9325 section 4.2 recommends, all ECDHE with AES-GCMRFC 10015 (July 2026) raises three of RFC 9325's "should not" rules to "must not" for TLS 1.2: static RSA key exchange, ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman and non-ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman. Non-ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman stays at "should not". RFC 9325 section 4.1 already forbids NULL and RC4 suites. Change the list only to remove suites.
Plain HTTPListener offThe OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet: "API-only endpoints should disable HTTP altogether and only support encrypted connections. When that is not possible, API endpoints should fail requests made over unencrypted HTTP connections instead of redirecting them." RFC 6797 section 7.2 says an HSTS host should answer plain HTTP with a permanent redirect. That advice is written for sites that people visit in a browser. Redirect only for those.
HSTSStrict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 on HTTPS responsesRFC 6797 section 6.1.1 requires the max-age directive and section 7.2 forbids sending the header over plain HTTP. RFC 9325 section 3.2 says web servers should use HSTS. The value is one year. RFC 6797 uses it in an example (section 6.2) and neither RFC recommends a figure, so the choice is this project's. It only affects clients that implement HSTS, which in practice means browsers. Start with a short max-age when a mistake would lock users out.
MethodsAn allowlist per route, TRACE offAPI8: "Be specific about which HTTP verbs each API can be accessed by: all other HTTP verbs should be disabled (e.g. HEAD)." RFC 9110 section 9.1 says "All general-purpose servers MUST support the methods GET and HEAD", so the lab keeps HEAD next to GET. If a browser calls the API across origins, the route also needs OPTIONS for the preflight.
CachingCache-Control: no-store on every responseRFC 9111 section 5.2.2.5: with no-store, "a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response". Relax it only for responses that hold nothing private and that you want cached.
Server bannerNo Server header, or a value with no versionRFC 9110 section 10.2.4 says an origin server should not send "needlessly fine-grained detail". The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet: "Remove this header or set non-informative values." Section 5 says how little this buys.
EnvironmentsIdentical settings, different credentials and hostnamesOWASP Top 10:2025 A02: "Development, QA, and production environments should all be configured identically, with different credentials used in each environment." List the settings that are meant to differ, and keep that list short.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves: that on the day of the audit, the running service refused each probe, and that its settings matched the baseline. That is all a clean audit says.

Doesn't prove the code is right. The lab's hardened API still fails on a booking id of abc. The configuration hides the detail and denies the request. It does not fix the missing input check. A10 says to catch errors where they occur and to keep a global handler "in case there is ever something we have missed". The handler is the backstop, not the fix.

Doesn't make a hidden version safe. RFC 9110 section 17.12 says that product information can in theory help an attacker, and then: "in practice, attackers tend to try all potential holes regardless of the apparent software versions being used". Removing the banner is cheap and worth doing. Patching is the control.

no-store is an instruction, not a guarantee. RFC 9111 says of it: "This directive is not a reliable or sufficient mechanism for ensuring privacy." A cache that is broken or hostile can ignore it.

A redirect and HSTS do not protect an API client. A redirect from http to https is an answer, and the server can only answer a request it has already received. The token in that request crossed the network in clear text first. HSTS exists to stop a browser sending that first request the next time, and it only works in a client that implements it. RFC 6797 section 14.2: "Non-conformant user agents ignore the Strict-Transport-Security header field". A script, a mobile app's HTTP library or another server will follow whatever URL it was configured with. Even a conformant client is exposed on its first visit, which RFC 6797 section 14.6 calls the bootstrap MITM vulnerability (MITM is short for man in the middle, an attacker placed between the client and the server). For an API, the control is that nothing answers on plain HTTP and every documented URL starts with https. A closed listener stops an attacker who can only watch the network. One who can answer in the server's place can still collect what a client sends to an http URL, which is why the client's URL is half of the control. Part D of the lab counts the tokens that leak each way.

Most browser security headers do nothing for a non-browser client. The OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet says that if an API is only consumed by non-browser clients, "most of these headers will have no effect since they are directives for browsers." Send the short list in section 3 anyway. It costs nothing, and you rarely know every client. Cookie attributes and request forgery belong to Module 28, Browser sessions, cookies and CSRF.

A comparison of two environments is not an audit. Two environments with the same wrong setting are identical. Part C of the lab shows two default installs that differ in nothing and have 15 findings each.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A hardened deployment must pass every one of these, in every environment. If one fails, the control is broken:

  • A request that makes the code raise an error returns a generic body with no stack trace, file path, query text or version, and the server log holds the detail under the identifier in the body.
  • A malformed, truncated or oversized credential is refused. It never falls through to the handler.
  • Every method that is not on a route's allowlist returns 405 with an Allow header, TRACE included, and has no effect. An unknown method returns 501.
  • /debug, sample pages and framework consoles return 404 on the public listener.
  • The vendor's default account is refused on every listener, and the management login is not reachable from the public listener at all.
  • A response with personal data carries Cache-Control: no-store, a correct Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
  • A connection to the plain HTTP port is refused. If a redirect is unavoidable, no HSTS header appears on the plain HTTP response.
  • A client that offers only TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 fails the handshake. No TLS 1.2 suite with static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange is selected.
  • A path written as //admin/login gets the same answer from the edge as /admin/login.
  • No component is behind its first fixed version.
  • The settings of each environment differ from the baseline only in the keys listed as per-environment, and the list is reviewed when it changes.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/misconfiguration_lab.py and run it with Python 3. It needs no packages beyond the standard library. On Windows, use py -3 wherever this page shows python3.

The API is a Python class driven by a configuration dict, and the auditor is a second class that calls it. The same application code runs in every part. Nothing opens a socket. TLS is a tuple of version names and a tuple of cipher suite names compared with the RFCs' rules, and no handshake takes place. The leaked error page is built from fixed strings, so it is not a real traceback, and the correlation ID is a counter where a real service would use a random value. The cipher suite check matches name prefixes, which is enough for the suites in the lab; RFC 10015 section 5 lists the affected suites one by one. The HSTS agent in Part D models two rules of RFC 6797: it notes a host from a header received over HTTPS (section 8.1) and rewrites http to https for a noted host (section 8.3). It does not follow redirects, and it leaves out includeSubDomains, max-age=0, preloaded lists and certificate errors. The vendor's default account is a placeholder pair, not any real product's default. Responses carry only the headers this module is about: RFC 9110 section 15.5.2 requires a 401 to carry WWW-Authenticate, and the lab's 401 does not.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
An API answers every plain HTTP request with a 301 to the https URL. A partner's script is configured with the http URL. What has the redirect protected?

Nothing in that request. The script sent its token in clear text, and the server could only redirect after it arrived. If the script follows the redirect, the call succeeds and nobody notices. Refusing the connection makes the mistake fail on the first test.

Your error responses now follow RFC 9457. Is the information leak fixed?

Not by the format. RFC 9457 defines where fields go. It does not stop a generator putting a stack trace in detail. The RFC says detail "ought to focus on helping the client correct the problem, rather than giving debugging information", and its security considerations say the details given must be scrutinized. The fix is what you put in the body, and one global handler so that no error path is missed.

Staging and production have identical configuration files. Is production hardened?

You do not know yet. They may be identical and wrong. Compare each with the written baseline, then probe the running service, because a setting can also be overridden at run time without the file changing.

RFC 9852 says new protocols must require TLS 1.3. Must you disable TLS 1.2 on an existing API today?

The RFC does not say so. It changes RFC 9325's rules for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported and TLS 1.2 may be. What every deployment must not do is negotiate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or SSL, and, since RFC 10015, select static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange in TLS 1.2. Dropping TLS 1.2 is a choice you make when your callers allow it.

sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/misconfiguration_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The published run prints 93 lines and ends all 80 lab checks passed. None of the edits needs a package.

1. The plain HTTP listener redirects

A partner complains that http URLs stopped working. In HARDENED, change "http_listener": "off" to "redirect".

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The lab exits 1. A redirect is an answer to a request that has already been sent, and the lab counts the credentials in those requests.
  • Check 49 does print 301, but check 58 still prints []. The auditor's plain-http probe only reports a listener that serves content with a 200. An audit finds what its probes look for, which is a reason to read them.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Checks 49 and 75 go from connection refused to 301, and checks 50 and 76 go from 0 to 1. The guest token crossed the network in clear text before the server could answer, and the full audit in check 58 did not notice. Check cfg-03 in the Reference layer asks for a refused connection for this reason.
  • That is the "serve" setting, which the default install uses. With "redirect" the booking is not in the reply. The token still was in the request.

2. Authentication errors are allowed through again

The token service has an outage, and someone decides the API should stay up when authentication code fails. In HARDENED, change "on_auth_error": "deny" to "allow".

How many checks fail, and what does check 56 print?

Every option, and why
  • Check 56 does print 200, but it is not alone. The setting is part of the baseline, so every environment built from it inherits the change, and the audits and the settings count see it too.
  • Correct. Exit 1, six failures. Check 56 goes from 500 to 200 and check 57 from False to True: the booking is in the body. Check 58 goes from [] to ['fail-open'], check 61 the same, check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'fail-open'], and check 64 from 17 to 16, because the baseline now agrees with the default install on one more setting. Check cfg-02 in the Reference layer is the rule this breaks.
  • A 401 would be a refusal. The "allow" branch returns a caller named unverified, which is not None, so the handler carries on and serves the booking.
  • The auditor sends one. Check 56 uses an Authorization header with a scheme and no token, which is all it takes.

3. The drifted setting is declared a per-environment difference

The comparison in Part C keeps reporting debug_errors. To quiet it, someone adds the key to the list of settings that are meant to differ:

PER_ENVIRONMENT_KEYS = ("hostname", "debug_errors")
What does Part C print now?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 60 goes from ['debug_errors'] to []. The comparison is now silent, and production still returns a stack trace, which the probe behind check 62 still finds. An exception list is itself configuration. Check cfg-10 in the Reference layer asks for it to be short and reviewed, and for the running service to be probed as well.
  • Check 62 does not read the list. It sends a request with a bad booking id to production and looks at the body that comes back.
  • Check 59 is the comparison with nothing left out, so it still prints ['debug_errors', 'hostname'].
  • The lab compares check 60 with the value it expects, so quieting the comparison fails the run.

4. TLS 1.1 is turned back on for one old client

In HARDENED, change "tls_versions": ("TLS1.2", "TLS1.3") to ("TLS1.1", "TLS1.2", "TLS1.3").

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 51 changes, and so does every audit of an environment built from this baseline.
  • Check 52 still prints protocol_version alert. The client in that check offers only TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.0 is still off.
  • Check 53 still prints TLS1.3. The lab's negotiate picks the highest version both sides have, and a client that offers TLS 1.2 and 1.3 is not affected by a lower version being enabled. The exposure is to clients that offer nothing better.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 51 goes from [] to ['TLS1.1'], checks 58 and 61 from [] to ['tls-versions'], and check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'tls-versions']. No request in the lab behaves differently, which is why this kind of change survives: nothing breaks, and one exception for one client becomes the setting for every environment. Check cfg-04 in the Reference layer is the rule.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • StandardOWASP API8:2023 says an API might be vulnerable if hardening is missing across any part of the API stack or cloud permissions are improperly configured, the latest security patches are missing, unnecessary features are enabled, "There are discrepancies in the way incoming requests are processed by servers in the HTTP server chain", TLS is missing, security or cache control directives are not sent to clients, a CORS policy is missing or improperly set, or error messages include stack traces or expose other sensitive information. It is an awareness document and sets no requirements. API8:2023, Is the API Vulnerable?
  • StandardOWASP API8:2023 says the API life cycle should include "A repeatable hardening process leading to fast and easy deployment of a properly locked down environment", a task to review and update configurations across the entire API stack, and "An automated process to continuously assess the effectiveness of the configuration and settings in all environments". It goes on to say: use an encrypted channel (TLS) for all API communications, internal or public-facing; be specific about which HTTP verbs each API can be accessed by and disable the others; for APIs that browser-based clients call, implement a proper CORS policy and include applicable security headers; restrict incoming content types and data formats; make all servers in the HTTP server chain process incoming requests in a uniform manner; and, where applicable, define and enforce all response payload schemas, error responses included. API8:2023, How To Prevent.
  • StandardRFC 9457 defines the problem details format and the application/problem+json media type. It says "Problem details are not a debugging tool for the underlying implementation" (section 4) and encourages generators that provide links to occurrence information "to avoid making implementation details such as a stack dump available through the HTTP interface" (section 5). It does not require an API to use the format. The OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet recommends that "a generic response is returned by the application but the error details are logged server side for investigation, and not returned to the user".
  • StandardAn origin server should answer 501 to a method it does not recognize or implement, and 405 to a method it implements but does not allow for the target resource (RFC 9110 section 9.1). It must generate an Allow header in a 405 response (RFC 9110 section 15.5.6). The final recipient of a TRACE request should exclude request fields that are likely to contain sensitive data when it generates the response (RFC 9110 section 9.3.8).
  • StandardImplementations must not negotiate SSL version 2, SSL version 3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1 (RFC 9325 section 3.1.1). "TLS 1.0 MUST NOT be used." and "TLS 1.1 MUST NOT be used." (RFC 8996 sections 4 and 5).
  • StandardRFC 9325 section 3.1.1 says implementations must support TLS 1.2, should support TLS 1.3, and must prefer TLS 1.3 when they implement it. RFC 9852 section 5 changes that for new protocols that use TLS: "this document mandates that TLS 1.3 MUST be supported for new protocols using TLS", and "this document says that TLS 1.2 MAY be supported as described above". The changes apply to TLS and not to DTLS.
  • StandardIn TLS 1.2 connections, clients must not offer and servers must not select cipher suites that use RSA key exchange, ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman, or non-ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman, and should not offer or select non-ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman (RFC 10015 sections 2, 3 and 4, with the changes to RFC 9325 tabulated in section 6). Implementations must not negotiate NULL or RC4 cipher suites (RFC 9325 section 4.1). RFC 9325 section 4.2 recommends four ECDHE suites with AES-GCM for TLS 1.2.
  • StandardService providers "SHOULD ensure that all servers providing the same service provide equivalent levels of security" in their TLS configuration, because an attacker might direct a client to the server that is easier to exploit (RFC 9325 section 3.9).
  • StandardWith the no-store response directive, "a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response". The same section says: "This directive is not a reliable or sufficient mechanism for ensuring privacy." RFC 9111 section 5.2.2.5. The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet recommends: "Use no-store for sensitive data to prevent any form of caching."
  • StandardAn HSTS host should include the Strict-Transport-Security field in responses sent over secure transport (RFC 6797 section 7.1) and must not include it in responses sent over non-secure transport (section 7.2). A user agent must ignore the field when it arrives over insecure transport (section 8.1). Web servers should use HSTS unless it would weaken security in their deployment (RFC 9325 section 3.2).
  • StandardA sender that generates a message containing content should generate a Content-Type header unless the media type is unknown to it (RFC 9110 section 8.3). An origin server should not generate a Server header "containing needlessly fine-grained detail" (RFC 9110 section 10.2.4). The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet recommends X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff together with a correct Content-Type.
  • StandardThe OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet recommends that API-only endpoints disable HTTP altogether, or fail requests made over unencrypted HTTP "instead of redirecting them". The OWASP REST Security Cheat Sheet recommends an allowlist of permitted HTTP methods with a 405 for everything else, and says to avoid exposing management endpoints via the internet. Cheat sheets are guidance and set no requirements.
  • StandardOWASP Top 10:2025 A10 names failing open among the scenarios it covers and says that part way through a transaction "it is extremely important that you roll back every part of the transaction and start again (also known as failing closed)". OWASP Top 10:2025 A02 lists "Default accounts and their passwords are still enabled and unchanged." among its conditions. Both are awareness documents and set no requirements.
  • BaselineOne global exception handler returns application/problem+json with type about:blank, the status, the standard title and an instance that carries a correlation ID. The exception is logged under the same ID and nowhere else.
  • BaselineAn error inside an authentication or authorization check denies the request. No setting exists that turns such an error into "allowed".
  • BaselineThe plain HTTP listener of an API is off. TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 are enabled, nothing older, with the four TLS 1.2 suites RFC 9325 section 4.2 recommends.
  • BaselineEach route has a method allowlist. TRACE, debug endpoints, sample content and default accounts are off in every environment, not only in production.
  • BaselineEvery response carries Cache-Control: no-store, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and, when it has content, a correct Content-Type. No response names a product version.
  • BaselineEvery environment is built from one baseline. The settings allowed to differ are listed by name. An automated audit compares each environment with the baseline and probes the running service.
  • OptionOffer only TLS 1.3 once every caller supports it. RFC 9325 section 1 names this as a decision a service provider might make.
  • OptionRedirect plain HTTP to HTTPS and send HSTS when people reach the same host in a browser. Keep API hosts and browser-facing hosts separate so the API host can refuse.
  • OptionPublish a security.txt file so that someone who finds a misconfiguration knows where to report it. RFC 9116 defines the format.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • No error response carries a stack trace, query text, file path or version One global handler returns a generic body with a correlation ID, and the detail is logged on the server under the same ID.
  • An error inside a security check denies the request Test with malformed and truncated credentials. No configuration setting turns an authentication or authorization error into access.
  • Plain HTTP is refused, and every hop uses TLS The API's HTTP listener is off, not redirecting, and internal connections between components are encrypted as well.
  • SSL, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are disabled and TLS 1.3 is offered No TLS 1.2 suite uses static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and every server for the same service has the same TLS settings.
  • Each route allows only the methods it needs Everything else returns 405 with an Allow header and has no effect. TRACE is off.
  • Debug endpoints, sample content and default accounts are gone Management functions are on a listener the internet cannot reach, with their own authentication, in every environment.
  • Sensitive responses carry Cache-Control: no-store Every response with content has a correct Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and no response names a product version.
  • Every server in the chain reads a request the same way Test path, method and header variants through the edge and compare them with what the backend does with the same bytes.
  • No component is behind its first fixed version The comparison runs on a schedule against vendor advisories, for the framework, the server and the TLS library.
  • Every environment is built from one baseline and audited automatically The audit compares settings with the baseline and probes the running service. The list of settings allowed to differ is short and reviewed.

DecisionStarting defaultWhat the sources say, and when to change it
Error bodyRFC 9457 problem details with type about:blank, the status, the standard title and an instance that carries the correlation IDRFC 9457 defines a format. It does not require an API to use it: section 1 says problem details "are (naturally) not the only way to convey the details of a problem in HTTP". What it does say about content is in section 4, "Problem details are not a debugging tool for the underlying implementation", and section 5 encourages generators that provide links to occurrence information to avoid making a stack dump available through the HTTP interface. Define your own problem types for errors a client can act on. The correlation ID is this project's use of instance, which the RFC defines as a URI reference that identifies the specific occurrence.
Minimum TLS versionTLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 enabled, nothing olderRFC 9325 section 3.1.1 says implementations must not negotiate SSL 2, SSL 3, TLS 1.0 or TLS 1.1. RFC 8996 sections 4 and 5 say the same of TLS 1.0 and 1.1. Drop TLS 1.2 once every caller supports 1.3: RFC 9325 section 1 says a provider "might decide to disable TLS 1.2 entirely and offer only TLS 1.3."
TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2 supportOffer TLS 1.3 and prefer itRFC 9325 section 3.1.1, as published in 2022, says implementations must support TLS 1.2 and should support TLS 1.3, and must prefer 1.3 when they have it. RFC 9852 (July 2026) changes two of those for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported, and TLS 1.2 may be. Its rule is addressed to protocol specifications: "Any new protocol that uses TLS MUST specify TLS 1.3 as its default." It does not tell an existing HTTP API to turn TLS 1.2 off. TLS 1.3 itself is RFC 9846.
TLS 1.2 cipher suitesThe four suites RFC 9325 section 4.2 recommends, all ECDHE with AES-GCMRFC 10015 (July 2026) raises three of RFC 9325's "should not" rules to "must not" for TLS 1.2: static RSA key exchange, ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman and non-ephemeral finite field Diffie-Hellman. Non-ephemeral elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman stays at "should not". RFC 9325 section 4.1 already forbids NULL and RC4 suites. Change the list only to remove suites.
Plain HTTPListener offThe OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet: "API-only endpoints should disable HTTP altogether and only support encrypted connections. When that is not possible, API endpoints should fail requests made over unencrypted HTTP connections instead of redirecting them." RFC 6797 section 7.2 says an HSTS host should answer plain HTTP with a permanent redirect. That advice is written for sites that people visit in a browser. Redirect only for those.
HSTSStrict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000 on HTTPS responsesRFC 6797 section 6.1.1 requires the max-age directive and section 7.2 forbids sending the header over plain HTTP. RFC 9325 section 3.2 says web servers should use HSTS. The value is one year. RFC 6797 uses it in an example (section 6.2) and neither RFC recommends a figure, so the choice is this project's. It only affects clients that implement HSTS, which in practice means browsers. Start with a short max-age when a mistake would lock users out.
MethodsAn allowlist per route, TRACE offAPI8: "Be specific about which HTTP verbs each API can be accessed by: all other HTTP verbs should be disabled (e.g. HEAD)." RFC 9110 section 9.1 says "All general-purpose servers MUST support the methods GET and HEAD", so the lab keeps HEAD next to GET. If a browser calls the API across origins, the route also needs OPTIONS for the preflight.
CachingCache-Control: no-store on every responseRFC 9111 section 5.2.2.5: with no-store, "a cache MUST NOT store any part of either the immediate request or the response". Relax it only for responses that hold nothing private and that you want cached.
Server bannerNo Server header, or a value with no versionRFC 9110 section 10.2.4 says an origin server should not send "needlessly fine-grained detail". The OWASP HTTP Headers Cheat Sheet: "Remove this header or set non-informative values." Section 5 says how little this buys.
EnvironmentsIdentical settings, different credentials and hostnamesOWASP Top 10:2025 A02: "Development, QA, and production environments should all be configured identically, with different credentials used in each environment." List the settings that are meant to differ, and keep that list short.

checks.title: No error response carries a stack trace, query text, file path or version
checks.detail: One global handler returns a generic body with a correlation ID, and the detail is logged on the server under the same ID.

checks.title: An error inside a security check denies the request
checks.detail: Test with malformed and truncated credentials. No configuration setting turns an authentication or authorization error into access.

checks.title: Plain HTTP is refused, and every hop uses TLS
checks.detail: The API's HTTP listener is off, not redirecting, and internal connections between components are encrypted as well.

checks.title: SSL, TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are disabled and TLS 1.3 is offered
checks.detail: No TLS 1.2 suite uses static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and every server for the same service has the same TLS settings.

checks.title: Each route allows only the methods it needs
checks.detail: Everything else returns 405 with an Allow header and has no effect. TRACE is off.

checks.title: Debug endpoints, sample content and default accounts are gone
checks.detail: Management functions are on a listener the internet cannot reach, with their own authentication, in every environment.

checks.title: Sensitive responses carry Cache-Control: no-store
checks.detail: Every response with content has a correct Content-Type and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and no response names a product version.

checks.title: Every server in the chain reads a request the same way
checks.detail: Test path, method and header variants through the edge and compare them with what the backend does with the same bytes.

checks.title: No component is behind its first fixed version
checks.detail: The comparison runs on a schedule against vendor advisories, for the framework, the server and the TLS library.

checks.title: Every environment is built from one baseline and audited automatically
checks.detail: The audit compares settings with the baseline and probes the running service. The list of settings allowed to differ is short and reviewed.

details.summary: An API answers every plain HTTP request with a 301 to the https URL. A partner's script is configured with the http URL. What has the redirect protected?
details.html:
An API answers every plain HTTP request with a 301 to the https URL. A partner's script is configured with the http URL. What has the redirect protected?

Nothing in that request. The script sent its token in clear text, and the server could only redirect after it arrived. If the script follows the redirect, the call succeeds and nobody notices. Refusing the connection makes the mistake fail on the first test.

details.summary: Your error responses now follow RFC 9457. Is the information leak fixed?
details.html:
Your error responses now follow RFC 9457. Is the information leak fixed?

Not by the format. RFC 9457 defines where fields go. It does not stop a generator putting a stack trace in detail. The RFC says detail "ought to focus on helping the client correct the problem, rather than giving debugging information", and its security considerations say the details given must be scrutinized. The fix is what you put in the body, and one global handler so that no error path is missed.

details.summary: Staging and production have identical configuration files. Is production hardened?
details.html:
Staging and production have identical configuration files. Is production hardened?

You do not know yet. They may be identical and wrong. Compare each with the written baseline, then probe the running service, because a setting can also be overridden at run time without the file changing.

details.summary: RFC 9852 says new protocols must require TLS 1.3. Must you disable TLS 1.2 on an existing API today?
details.html:
RFC 9852 says new protocols must require TLS 1.3. Must you disable TLS 1.2 on an existing API today?

The RFC does not say so. It changes RFC 9325's rules for new protocols that use TLS: TLS 1.3 must be supported and TLS 1.2 may be. What every deployment must not do is negotiate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 or SSL, and, since RFC 10015, select static RSA or finite field Diffie-Hellman key exchange in TLS 1.2. Dropping TLS 1.2 is a choice you make when your callers allow it.

Every option, and why
  • The lab exits 1. A redirect is an answer to a request that has already been sent, and the lab counts the credentials in those requests.
  • Check 49 does print 301, but check 58 still prints []. The auditor's plain-http probe only reports a listener that serves content with a 200. An audit finds what its probes look for, which is a reason to read them.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Checks 49 and 75 go from connection refused to 301, and checks 50 and 76 go from 0 to 1. The guest token crossed the network in clear text before the server could answer, and the full audit in check 58 did not notice. Check cfg-03 in the Reference layer asks for a refused connection for this reason.
  • That is the "serve" setting, which the default install uses. With "redirect" the booking is not in the reply. The token still was in the request.

Every option, and why
  • Check 56 does print 200, but it is not alone. The setting is part of the baseline, so every environment built from it inherits the change, and the audits and the settings count see it too.
  • Correct. Exit 1, six failures. Check 56 goes from 500 to 200 and check 57 from False to True: the booking is in the body. Check 58 goes from [] to ['fail-open'], check 61 the same, check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'fail-open'], and check 64 from 17 to 16, because the baseline now agrees with the default install on one more setting. Check cfg-02 in the Reference layer is the rule this breaks.
  • A 401 would be a refusal. The "allow" branch returns a caller named unverified, which is not None, so the handler carries on and serves the booking.
  • The auditor sends one. Check 56 uses an Authorization header with a scheme and no token, which is all it takes.

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 60 goes from ['debug_errors'] to []. The comparison is now silent, and production still returns a stack trace, which the probe behind check 62 still finds. An exception list is itself configuration. Check cfg-10 in the Reference layer asks for it to be short and reviewed, and for the running service to be probed as well.
  • Check 62 does not read the list. It sends a request with a bad booking id to production and looks at the body that comes back.
  • Check 59 is the comparison with nothing left out, so it still prints ['debug_errors', 'hostname'].
  • The lab compares check 60 with the value it expects, so quieting the comparison fails the run.

Every option, and why
  • Check 51 changes, and so does every audit of an environment built from this baseline.
  • Check 52 still prints protocol_version alert. The client in that check offers only TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.0 is still off.
  • Check 53 still prints TLS1.3. The lab's negotiate picks the highest version both sides have, and a client that offers TLS 1.2 and 1.3 is not affected by a lower version being enabled. The exposure is to clients that offer nothing better.
  • Correct. Exit 1, four failures. Check 51 goes from [] to ['TLS1.1'], checks 58 and 61 from [] to ['tls-versions'], and check 62 from ['error-detail'] to ['error-detail', 'tls-versions']. No request in the lab behaves differently, which is why this kind of change survives: nothing breaks, and one exception for one client becomes the setting for every environment. Check cfg-04 in the Reference layer is the rule.
